items.text: Anil Seth argues that machine consciousness is not an inevitable next step in AI progress, and that treating it as one confuses two very different things: intelligence and consciousness.

Seth's stakes: if AI systems are conscious, they have moral status and can suffer. If we only believe they're conscious, our ethics and psychology can be distorted either way. Getting this wrong costs something real either direction.

Seth traces our eagerness to see conscious AI to psychological biases, not evidence: anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism, and anthropomorphism all make us project mindedness onto anything that seems humanlike.

Language is especially seductive, Seth writes. Nobody calls AlphaFold conscious, but chatbots that talk like us trigger the intuition instantly. Even calling AI errors 'hallucinations' smuggles in an assumption of experience.
Seth also flags exponential-growth thinking and 'techno-rapture' hopes of digital immortality as further pulls toward believing conscious AI is imminent, independent of whether it's actually likely.
Seth's core target is computational functionalism: the assumption that the right computation is sufficient for consciousness. He calls this an unexamined assumption, not a settled fact.

First argument: brains aren't Turing machines made of meat. Seth says brain function is inseparable from its living material, unlike software cleanly detachable from hardware — so 'substrate independence' may not hold.
Second argument: digital computation itself is limited. Continuous, stochastic, richly temporal processes in real brains may not be capturable as algorithms at all, Seth writes, even in principle.

Third argument, more speculative by Seth's own admission: consciousness may require being alive. He links perceptual prediction and bodily self-regulation to the autopoietic, metabolic nature of living cells.

Fourth argument: simulation isn't instantiation. A simulated brain, however detailed, only produces consciousness if computational functionalism is already true — an assumption, Seth notes, mind-uploading dreams quietly depend on.

Seth stresses genuine uncertainty: no theory of consciousness has consensus, and no test can settle whether an AI is truly conscious. His practical stance: don't try to build conscious AI, but also don't ignore convincingly conscious-seeming AI, which raises separate ethical dangers either way.

Seth closes by warning against mechanizing our self-understanding: mistaking ourselves for our machines, he writes, makes us overestimate them and underestimate the embodied, living, breathing thing consciousness actually is.
Seth leaves open which alternative technologies, if any, might someday meet his conditions for consciousness, and how societies should navigate AI systems that merely seem conscious in the meantime.
